idiom_name: type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; radius: number } | ... + switch on both kind fields
implementation_notes: TypeScript types are erased at runtime, so dispatch always runs on a runtime tag the data carries: model both hierarchies as discriminated unions and switch on `a.kind` first, then on `b.kind`, and the compiler narrows each member inside its case. With a closed switch plus a never-typed assertion the missing pair becomes a type error, which is the visitor's compile-time guarantee recovered statically and free of the accept/visit round-trip. The classic visitor class structure (see visitor-class) remains the option when element types must be extensible by consumers or operations have to be first-class objects.
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness is opt-in: without a never-typed fallback (or strict return checks) a missing case silently returns undefined.
Narrowing is compile-time only: data entering from JSON or a network call must be validated into the union, otherwise an unexpected kind matches nothing.
instanceof breaks across module boundaries or duplicated package copies: a discriminant field is more reliable than constructor identity.

variants.name: Visitor interface + accept() round-trip
variants.implementation_notes: The classic structure works unchanged in TypeScript - interfaces, classes and two dynamic dispatches - and the compiler checks that every visitor implements every declared method, so adding an element type breaks all visitors. Because TypeScript has no method overloading, the visit method names must encode the element type (visitCircle/visitSquare), exactly as in JavaScript. This variant fits libraries whose consumers extend the element set (AST tooling, code generators) where a closed discriminated union would freeze the set, and where operations should be enumerable as objects.
pitfalls: Method names must be unique per element type (no overloading), so the visitor interface is a naming contract and a wrong name only fails if it still satisfies the interface.
A generic visitShape(shape: Shape) method reintroduces silent fallbacks: omit it.
Interfaces do not exist at runtime: the element hierarchy must be constructed with classes or factories so that accept is actually callable.
